formal_models.name: CSS rule structure
formal_models.expression: stylesheet → rule → selector(s) + declaration block → property:value
formal_models.mechanism: Selectors determine targets; declarations assign values.

formal_models.name: Cascade resolution
formal_models.expression: matching declarations → priority/importance → specificity → source order → selected value
formal_models.mechanism: The cascade resolves competing declarations using priority and tie-break rules.

formal_models.name: Selector matching
formal_models.mechanism: Selectors can use element type, IDs, classes, attributes, relationships, pseudo-classes, and pseudo-elements.

formal_models.name: Inheritance
formal_models.mechanism: Some properties inherit from ancestors when not overridden.

formal_models.name: Box model
formal_models.expression: content + padding + border + margin → box geometry
formal_models.mechanism: Element dimensions and surrounding spacing determine layout geometry.

formal_models.name: External stylesheet reuse
formal_models.expression: HTML → link stylesheet → shared CSS → rules applied across pages
formal_models.mechanism: A common stylesheet reduces repetition and can be cached.

formal_models.name: Responsive presentation
formal_models.expression: viewport/device/media → media query → selected rules → adapted layout
formal_models.mechanism: Conditional styling changes presentation across screens, orientations, and output media.

formal_models.name: Browser compatibility workflow
formal_models.expression: feature → support data → cross-browser test → @supports/fallback → resilient output
formal_models.mechanism: Compatibility information and fallbacks reduce browser-specific failures.

formal_models.name: Preprocessor compilation
formal_models.expression: Sass/Less/Stylus source → compiler → CSS → browser rendering
formal_models.mechanism: Preprocessors provide authoring abstractions but the browser receives CSS.

formal_models.name: Multi-medium presentation
formal_models.expression: semantic markup → user/media-specific styles → screen/print/speech/Braille output
formal_models.mechanism: Separation permits the same content to be presented in different forms.

formal_models.name: Framework styling
formal_models.expression: framework stylesheet → reusable patterns → page layout
formal_models.mechanism: Frameworks accelerate common design tasks but may introduce unused CSS overhead.

formal_models.name: Presentational markup migration
formal_models.expression: repeated HTML formatting → shared CSS rules → simpler markup
formal_models.mechanism: Moving style declarations out of markup reduces duplication and maintenance effort.

source_claims.claim: CSS specifies presentation of markup documents and is a core Web technology alongside HTML and JavaScript.
CSS separates content/structure from presentation, enabling reuse, maintainability, caching, accessibility, and alternate media.
CSS rules pair selectors with declaration blocks containing property-value declarations.
Selectors match elements by type, ID, class, attributes, relationships, state, and partial/generated content.
The cascade resolves competing declarations using priority, specificity, order, inheritance, and defaults.
CSS controls layout, dimensions, spacing, borders, typography, responsive design, and visual effects.
CSS can provide distinct presentation for screen, print, speech, Braille, and mobile contexts.
CSS originated in 1990s style-sheet proposals and CSS Level 1 was released in December 1996.
CSS 3 is developed as separate modules and summarized in periodic snapshots.
Browser differences are addressed with testing, feature queries, support tables, and fallbacks.
The source describes limitations involving scope, pseudo-class control, rule naming/composition, and arbitrary text targeting.
The ecosystem includes preprocessors, frameworks, extensions, and organization methodologies.

semantic_distinctions.distinction: HTML defines structure/content; CSS defines presentation.
CSS controls styling/layout; JavaScript supplies behavior.
Selectors choose targets; declarations set property values.
Pseudo-classes describe state/context; pseudo-elements target generated or partial content.
An ID identifies a single document element; classes can be reused.
Cascade resolves competing declarations; inheritance passes eligible values from ancestors.
Specificity compares selector weights; source order is a tie-breaker.
Inline declarations attach to one element; external CSS centralizes reusable rules.
Absolute units use fixed reference measures; relative units depend on context.
Responsive styles adapt to viewport/device context.
CSS 3 is modular; the source rejects a single monolithic CSS 4 release.
Sass, Less, and Stylus add authoring abstractions and compile to CSS.
Frameworks speed development but can add unused features and overhead.
Prefixes historically targeted browser-specific behavior; @supports tests support conditions.
Separating presentation lets the same content be adapted to different media.
Some style-reuse limitations can be addressed by languages compiling to CSS.

misconceptions.correction: HTML defines structure; CSS specifies presentation.

misconceptions.misconception: A CSS class is itself a CSS subsystem feature.
misconceptions.correction: The class attribute belongs to the markup model; CSS selectors match its value.
Pseudo-classes match state/context; pseudo-elements target generated or partial content.

misconceptions.misconception: The last CSS rule always wins.
misconceptions.correction: Importance and specificity can take precedence over source order.
Specificity components are compared as separate weights.
Only properties that inherit by their rules receive ancestor values.

misconceptions.misconception: ID and class selectors are interchangeable.
misconceptions.correction: IDs identify a document element; classes can be reused.

misconceptions.misconception: CSS is only for screen visuals.
misconceptions.correction: CSS can tailor print and source-described speech/Braille contexts.

misconceptions.misconception: CSS 4 is one unified version after CSS 3.
misconceptions.correction: The source describes CSS 3 as modules rather than a monolithic CSS 4.
Browser-specific prefixes do not eliminate testing or fallback needs.

misconceptions.misconception: Framework CSS is always smaller than handcrafted CSS.
misconceptions.correction: Frameworks may include unused styles and add download/maintenance overhead.
Sass, Less, and Stylus compile to CSS processed by browsers.

misconceptions.misconception: Inline styles are best for site-wide consistency.
misconceptions.correction: External stylesheets centralize reusable rules and can be cached.
Responsive styles adapt layout to device, viewport, and orientation.
Polyfills are JavaScript code that may emulate unsupported Web behavior.
The source lists scoping, rule naming/composition, hover-control, and text-targeting limitations.
